claim: Generating recombinant monoclonal antibodies (R-mAbs) from mAb-producing hybridomas offers numerous advantages that increase the effectiveness, reproducibility, and transparent reporting of research.
source: Generating recombinant monoclonal antibodies (R-mAbs) from mAb-producing hybridomas offers numerous advantages that increase the effectiveness, reproducibility, and transparent reporting of research.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract supported by the broader literature context cited throughout the manuscript.

claim: The authors cloned immunoglobulin G (IgG) variable domains from cryopreserved hybridoma cells.
source: We cloned immunoglobulin G (IgG) variable domains from cryopreserved hybridoma cells and input them into an integrated pipeline for expression and validation of functional R-mAbs.
evidence: The manuscript describes the methodology and results of cloning IgG variable domains from cryopreserved hybridomas.

claim: The authors eliminated aberrant Sp2/0-Ag14 hybridoma-derived variable light transcripts using restriction enzyme treatment.
source: To improve efficiency over standard protocols, we eliminated aberrant Sp2/0-Ag14 hybridoma-derived variable light transcripts using restriction enzyme treatment.
evidence: The manuscript describes using BciVI restriction enzyme digestion to eliminate aberrant light chains, with data shown in Figure 2E and Table 1.

claim: The authors engineered a plasmid backbone that allows for switching of the IgG subclasses without altering target binding specificity.
source: Further, we engineered a plasmid backbone that allows for switching of the IgG subclasses without altering target binding specificity to generate R-mAbs useful in simultaneous multiplex labeling experiments not previously possible.
evidence: The manuscript describes generation of IgG2a expression plasmid and validation of subclass-switched R-mAbs in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The method was employed to rescue IgG variable sequences and generate functional R-mAbs from a non-viable cryopreserved hybridoma.
source: The method was also employed to rescue IgG variable sequences and generate functional R-mAbs from a non-viable cryopreserved hybridoma.
evidence: The manuscript describes recovery of functional D3/71R R-mAb from non-viable hybridoma cells, shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: All R-mAb sequences and plasmids will be archived and disseminated from open source suppliers.
source: All R-mAb sequences and plasmids will be archived and disseminated from open source suppliers.
evidence: The manuscript states that plasmids will be deposited at Addgene.

claim: Production of Abs in a renewable form, such as monoclonal antibodies (mAbs), represents a substantial advance over polyclonal Abs from antisera.
source: It is widely recognized that production of Abs in a renewable form, such as monoclonal antibodies (mAbs), represents a substantial advance over polyclonal Abs from antisera that are available in finite quantity, and that comprise a heterogeneous and less definable population of Abs (Harlow and Lane, 1988; Greenfield, 2014; Busby et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Having mAbs available in recombinant form as recombinant mAbs (R-mAbs) offers numerous additional advantages.
source: Having mAbs available in recombinant form as recombinant mAbs (R-mAbs) offers numerous additional advantages (Bradbury and Plückthun, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bradbury and Plückthun, 2015.

claim: Recombinant expression systems allow for the reliable production of an R-mAb not prone to loss by genetic instability of tetra- or hexa-ploid hybridoma cells or other factors.
source: Recombinant expression systems allow for the reliable production of an R-mAb not prone to loss by genetic instability of tetra- or hexa-ploid hybridoma cells or other factors (Andreeff et al., 1985; Barnes et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Andreeff et al., 1985 and Barnes et al., 2003.

claim: Unlike hybridoma cell lines that can express multiple functional heavy and light immunoglobulin chains, recombinant expression ensures production of a single, molecularly defined R-mAb.
source: Moreover, unlike hybridoma cell lines that can express multiple functional heavy and light immunoglobulin chains (Zack et al., 1995; Blatt et al., 1998; Bradbury et al., 2018), recombinant expression ensures production of a single, molecularly defined R-mAb.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Zack et al., 1995; Blatt et al., 1998; Bradbury et al., 2018.

claim: Recombinant expression can yield production levels hundreds or even thousands of times higher than is possible with endogenous expressions of mAbs from hybridoma cells.
source: Recombinant expression can also yield production levels hundreds or even thousands of times higher than is possible with endogenous expressions of mAbs from hybridoma cells (e.g., Backliwal et al., 2008; Fischer et al., 2015; Kunert and Reinhart, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Backliwal et al., 2008; Fischer et al., 2015; Kunert and Reinhart, 2016.

claim: The cloning of R-mAbs provides for permanent, dependable and inexpensive archiving of the R-mAb as plasmid DNA and nucleic acid sequences versus an archiving system relying on expensive cryopreservation of hybridoma cell lines in liquid nitrogen.
source: Furthermore, the cloning of R-mAbs provides for permanent, dependable and inexpensive archiving of the R-mAb as plasmid DNA and nucleic acid sequences versus an archiving system relying on expensive cryopreservation of hybridoma cell lines in liquid nitrogen, and their subsequent recovery as viable cell cultures.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the properties of DNA versus living cells.

claim: Mouse mAbs of distinct IgG subclasses can be robustly, reliably and specifically detected with commercial subclass-specific secondary antibodies.
source: Mouse mAbs of distinct IgG subclasses can be robustly, reliably and specifically detected with commercial subclass-specific secondary antibodies, and, as such, can be multiplexed in a manner analogous to Abs from different species (e.g., Bekele-Arcuri et al., 1996; Rhodes et al., 1997; Lim et al., 2000; Rasband et al., 2001; Manning et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Mouse mAb collections generally have an extremely high representation (≈70%) of IgG1 mAbs.
source: One limitation to greater adoption of this approach is that mouse mAb collections generally have an extremely high representation (≈70%) of IgG1 mAbs (Manning et al., 2012), which limits the flexibility of multiplex labeling.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Manning et al., 2012 and data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The conversion of mAbs into R-mAbs allows for their subsequent engineering into forms with properties distinct from their parent mAb.
source: The conversion of mAbs into R-mAbs allows for their subsequent engineering into forms with properties distinct from their parent mAb, as is routinely done to impact diverse aspects, including target binding affinity, of therapeutic R-mAbs (Kennedy et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kennedy et al., 2018.

claim: The authors previously generated a large library of mouse mAbs that have been extensively validated for efficacy and specificity for immunolabeling endogenous target proteins in mammalian brain samples.
source: We previously generated a large library of mouse mAbs that have been extensively validated for efficacy and specificity for immunolabeling endogenous target proteins in mammalian brain samples in immunoblotting (IB) and immunohistochemistry (IHC) applications (Bekele-Arcuri et al., 1996; Rhodes and Trimmer, 2006; Gong et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior publications from the authors' group.

claim: The authors cloned directly from cryopreserved hybridomas, without the need for their labor-intensive recovery into cell culture.
source: For the cloning steps, we built upon a previously described method (Crosnier et al., 2010; Müller-Sienerth et al., 2014) to clone IgG VH and VL region sequences, but with the modification that we cloned directly from cryopreserved hybridomas, without the need for their labor-intensive recovery into cell culture.
evidence: The manuscript describes the methodology of extracting RNA directly from cryopreserved cells.

claim: The authors employed PCR-mediated amplification to generate IgG VH and VL region sequences from hybridoma-derived cDNA.
source: Our overall cloning strategy (Figure 1A) employs PCR-mediated amplification to generate IgG VH and VL region sequences from hybridoma-derived cDNA, followed by PCR-based fusion of these VH and VL regions with a joining fragment that contains a subset of the elements needed for high level expression of R-mAbs from transfected mammalian cell lines.
evidence: The methodology is described in text and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The authors used a degenerate mouse Ig variable region primer set that at the time of design recognized 97% and 98% of known functional heavy and kappa (κ) light chain sequences, respectively.
source: We amplified the IgG VL kappa (κ) and VH domain sequences from the hybridoma cDNA templates using a degenerate mouse Ig variable region primer set developed by Gavin Wright and colleagues (Crosnier et al., 2010). This expanded on a previously used set (Krebber et al., 1997) that at the time of their design recognized 97% and 98% of known functional heavy and kappa (κ) light chain sequences, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Crosnier et al., 2010 and Krebber et al., 1997.

claim: Lambda light chains constitute only a small percentage of light chains used in mouse immunoglobulins.
source: Lambda light chains were not targeted for amplification because they constitute only a small percentage of light chains used in mouse immunoglobulins (Haughton et al., 1978; Woloschak and Krco, 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Haughton et al., 1978 and Woloschak and Krco, 1987.

claim: PCR amplification reliably gave products of the expected 360 base pairs (bp) for both the VL and VH domain sequences.
source: This PCR amplification reliably gave products of the expected 360 base pairs (bp) for both the VL and VH domain sequences, examples of which are shown in Figure 2A for representative mAbs N59/36 ('N59', anti-NR2B/GRIN2B glutamate receptor) and K39/25 ('K39', anti-Kv2.1/KCNB1 potassium channel).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A major obstacle in cloning functionally rearranged IgG sequences from many mouse hybridomas is the presence of an aberrant kappa IgG light chain transcript expressed by the Sp2/0-Ag14 (Sp2/0) hybridoma.
source: A major obstacle in cloning functionally rearranged IgG sequences from many mouse hybridomas is the presence of an aberrant kappa IgG light chain transcript expressed by the Sp2/0-Ag14 (Sp2/0) hybridoma (Carroll et al., 1988) that frequently serves as a 'myeloma' partner for fusion with mouse splenocytes to generate mAb-producing hybridomas (Shulman et al., 1978), and that was used as the fusion partner in all of our mAb generation efforts (Bekele-Arcuri et al., 1996; Gong et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Carroll et al., 1988; Shulman et al., 1978; Bekele-Arcuri et al., 1996; Gong et al., 2016.

claim: The source of the non-productive IgG light chain is the MOPC-21 myeloma cell line used to generate the Sp2/0 hybridoma.
source: The source of this non-productive IgG light chain is the MOPC-21 myeloma cell line used to generate the Sp2/0 hybridoma (Shulman et al., 1978).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Shulman et al., 1978.

claim: Aberrant chain mRNA expression varies greatly among distinct hybridoma cell lines but in certain cases can exceed the levels of functional light chain transcripts.
source: As we experienced, and as previously reported by others (Carroll et al., 1988), aberrant chain mRNA expression varies greatly among distinct hybridoma cell lines but in certain cases can exceed the levels of functional light chain transcripts.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Carroll et al., 1988 and the authors' own observations.

claim: The authors treated VL PCR products with the restriction enzyme BciVI to eliminate the aberrant Sp2/0-derived transcript.
source: As such, we sought to eliminate this aberrant light chain during the cloning process. We treated the VL PCR products with the restriction enzyme BciVI.
evidence: The methodology is described in the text and results shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The restriction site for BciVI is present in the VL region of the aberrant Sp2/0-derived transcript, but is predicted to occur at a low frequency in functional mouse VL kappa sequences.
source: The restriction site for this enzyme is present in the VL region of the aberrant Sp2/0-derived transcript, but is predicted to occur at a low frequency in functional mouse VL kappa sequences (Juste et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Juste et al., 2006.

claim: VL PCR products from Sp2/0 cells were completely digested by BciVI, as shown by the decreased size from ≈360 bp to ≈180 bp.
source: Due to the exclusive presence of aberrant light chain in Sp2/0 cells, VL PCR products from these cells were completely digested, as shown by the decreased size of the VL PCR products from ≈360 bp typical of VL PCR products (see Figure 2A for examples) to the ≈180 bp fragment that results from BciVI digestion (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The sample prepared from pooled mouse splenocytes was not detectably affected by BciVI digestion.
source: In contrast, the sample prepared from the pooled mouse splenocytes was not detectably affected by BciVI digestion (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: After BciVI digestion was incorporated into the protocol, DNA sequencing of 149 colony PCR-positive clones from 26 different hybridomas revealed that only 12 (8%) still contained the aberrant Vk light chain.
source: After BciVI digestion was incorporated into the protocol, DNA sequencing of 149 colony PCR-positive clones from 26 different hybridomas revealed that only 12 (8%) still contained the aberrant Vk light chain (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: In rare cases (3/248 clones pursued), the BciVI restriction site was also present in functionally rearranged splenocyte-derived VL genes.
source: In certain cases, digestion of hybridoma VL PCR products resulted in fragments of unexpected sizes (see the K58/35 lane in Figure 2E), indicating, as predicted by an earlier bioinformatics analysis (Juste et al., 2006), that in rare cases (in our hands, 3/248 clones pursued to this step) the BciVI restriction site was also present in these functionally rearranged splenocyte-derived VL genes.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E and citation to Juste et al., 2006.

claim: For projects where splenocyte-derived Vk light chain PCR products were sensitive to BciVI digestion, cloning without BciVI treatment yielded somewhat lower frequency of clones that produced functional R-mAbs (≈37%) than those containing splenocyte-derived VL PCR products refractory to BciVI digestion (≈48%).
source: As one example, the splenocyte-derived Vk light chain PCR products from the K58/35 hybridoma were sensitive to BciVI digestion, which necessitated their cloning in the absence of the BciVI digestion step. This project yielded somewhat lower frequency of clones that produced functional R-mAbs able to detect target antigen (≈37%) than, on average, those containing splenocyte-derived VL PCR products refractory to BciVI digestion (≈48%; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data referenced in Supplementary file 1.

claim: On average, ≈93% of all clones subjected to restriction analysis passed this screening step.
source: On average, ≈93% of all clones subjected to restriction analysis passed this screening step.
evidence: This is a summary statistic from the authors' data.

claim: The authors selected the IF-ICC assay in transiently transfected heterologous cells for R-mAb validation because it is high-throughput, requires only a small amount of R-mAb sample, and the robust difference between target-expressing and non-expressing cells allows for sensitivity and clarity of results.
source: This method was chosen because it is high-throughput, employing 96 well microtiter plates, it requires only a small amount of R-mAb sample, and the robust difference between target-expressing and non-expressing cells in the same sample allows for sensitivity and clarity of results.
evidence: This is a methodological justification provided by the authors.

claim: In comparing the overall results from 180 recent projects that had BciVI-resistant splenocyte-derived VL PCR products, 72% (129 projects) yielded at least one positive R-mAb on their first pass through the pipeline.
source: In comparing the overall results from 180 recent projects that had BciVI-resistant splenocyte-derived VL PCR products, and that were taken through this entire pipeline one time (Supplementary file 1), we found that a range of 1–15 colony PCR- and restriction digest-positive candidate R-mAbs per project were evaluated in the COS-ICC assay (919 total, mean/project = 5.11 ± 0.23 S.E.M.). For these 180 projects, cloning was performed after BciVI digestion, and all restriction digest-validated candidates were tested for functional mAb production. Of these 180 projects, 72% (129 projects) yielded at least one positive R-mAb on their first pass through the pipeline.
evidence: This is a summary statistic from the authors' data referenced in Supplementary file 1.

claim: A retrospective analysis of 129 successful projects revealed an overall success rate of 48.4% for all 741 restriction digest-validated candidate R-mAbs tested.
source: A retrospective analysis of these 129 successful projects revealed a range of 1 to 13 restriction digest-validated candidates were evaluated (mean/project = 5.74 ± 0.26 S.E.M.), with an overall success rate of 48.4% for all 741 restriction digest-validated candidate R-mAbs tested.
evidence: This is a summary statistic from the authors' data.

claim: A statistically significant difference (two-tailed P value = 2.48×10−6) existed between the number of candidates evaluated in successful versus unsuccessful projects.
source: A statistically significant difference (two-tailed P value = 2.48×10−6) existed between the number of candidates evaluated in successful versus unsuccessful projects.
evidence: This is a statistical analysis result from the authors' data.

claim: The per-project COS-ICC rate success was impacted by number of clones tested: for 1–3 clones tested (66 projects), the project success rate was 50%, for 4–6 (62 projects) it was ≈ 77%, and for ≥7 (52 projects) it was ≈92%.
source: The per-project COS-ICC rate success was impacted by number of clones tested. For 1–3 clones tested (66 projects), the project success rate was 50%, for 4–6 (62 projects) it was ≈ 77%, and for ≥7 (52 projects) it was ≈92%.
evidence: This is a summary statistic from the authors' data.

claim: The per clone success rate was similar between the three bins (≈ 45% vs. ≈39% vs. ≈ 45%).
source: However, the per clone success rate was similar between the three bins (≈ 45% vs. ≈39% vs. ≈ 45%).
evidence: This is a summary statistic from the authors' data.

claim: The K28/43 mAb is widely used as a marker of excitatory synapses, with ≈520 publications citing its use as of 1/1/19.
source: This mAb is widely used as a marker of excitatory synapses (e.g., as of 1/1/19 ≈520 publications have cited the use of the K28/43 mAb as obtained from the UC Davis/NIH NeuroMab Facility alone).
evidence: This is a citation count provided by the authors.

claim: The K28/43 mAb is of the IgG2a subclass.
source: While the K28/43 mAb is already of a less common IgG subclass (IgG2a), generating a subclass switched version with an alternate IgG subclass would provide greater flexibility in its use in multiplex labeling experiments, and also provide proof of concept that we could use our process to effectively generate subclass switched R-mAbs with efficacy and specificity comparable to the parent mAb.
evidence: This is stated in the text.

claim: The authors generated VL and VH domain cDNA fragments from the cryopreserved K28/43 hybridoma and cloned them into the original P1316 plasmid that contains a mouse IgG1 CH domain.
source: We generated VL and VH domain cDNA fragments from the cryopreserved K28/43 hybridoma and cloned them into the original P1316 plasmid that contains a mouse IgG1 CH domain (Crosnier et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a description of the methodology used.

claim: The native K28/43 hybridoma-generated mAb exhibited a signal corresponding to the IgG2a subclass-specific secondary Ab with no detectable signal for the IgG1 subclass-specific secondary Ab.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, as expected, the sample receiving only the native K28/43 hybridoma-generated mAb exhibited a signal corresponding to the IgG2a subclass-specific secondary Ab (red) with no detectable signal for the IgG1 subclass-specific secondary Ab (green).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Labeling with the K28/43R R-mAb alone produced only an IgG1 subclass-specific green signal demonstrating a successful IgG subclass switch for the R-mAb.
source: Conversely, labeling with the K28/43R R-mAb alone produced only an IgG1 subclass-specific green signal demonstrating a successful IgG subclass switch for the R-mAb (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Simultaneous multiplex labeling with the hybridoma-generated mAb and a positive R-mAb resulted in an identical pattern of immunolabeling at the cellular level and at the subcellular level.
source: Simultaneous multiplex labeling with the hybridoma-generated mAb and a positive R-mAb resulted in an identical pattern of immunolabeling at the cellular level in the specific cells recognized, and at the subcellular level as to the pattern of immunolabeling within the labeled cells, as shown by the uniform hue of the signal in the merged panel, indicating that both the mAb and R-mAb were recognizing the same target (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The signal from the K28/43 mAb and the K28/43R R-mAb was indistinguishable in its laminar and subcellular pattern in cerebellar cortex.
source: As shown in Figure 3B, as detected with secondary Abs specific for their respective mouse IgG subclasses, the signal from these two primary antibodies was indistinguishable in its laminar and subcellular pattern in cerebellar cortex, consistent with previous studies of PSD-95 (e.g., Kistner et al., 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B and citation to Kistner et al., 1993.

claim: Both K28/43 mAb and K28/43R R-mAb signals were especially intense in the terminal pinceau of basket cells located adjacent to the Purkinje cell layer.
source: Both signals were especially intense in the terminal pinceau of basket cells located adjacent to the Purkinje cell layer, and both signals were also present in the molecular layer, and for the most part lacking in the granule cell layer (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The K28/43 R-mAb can be used reliably for multiplex immunolabeling of endogenous PSD-95 in brain sections.
source: This demonstrates that consistent with the validation in heterologous COS-1 cells expressing exogenous PSD-95, the K28/43 R-mAb can be used reliably for multiplex immunolabeling of endogenous PSD-95 in brain sections.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Both the IgG1 and IgG2a subclass isoforms of the K28/43R R-mAb gave identical immunolabeling patterns against samples from rat brain and COS-1 cells overexpressing PSD-95.
source: Both the IgG1 and IgG2a subclass isoforms of the K28/43R R-mAb gave identical immunolabeling patterns against samples from rat brain and COS-1 cells overexpressing PSD-95.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The pattern of R-mAb immunolabeling was similar to that obtained with the rabbit polyclonal antibody, and absent against samples of COS-1 cells exogenously expressing other MAGUK superfamily members.
source: Moreover, the pattern of R-mAb immunolabeling was similar to that obtained with the rabbit polyclonal antibody, and absent against samples of COS-1 cells exogenously expressing other MAGUK superfamily members (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The authors modified the P1316 plasmid by replacing the γ1 CH domain with a mouse γ2a CH domain.
source: To generate R-mAbs of less common mouse IgG subclasses, we modified this plasmid by replacing the γ1 CH domain with a mouse γ2a CH domain.
evidence: This is a description of the methodology used.

claim: The authors amplified the γ2a CH domain sequence from cDNA generated from the hybridomas producing the K28/43 IgG2a mAb.
source: We amplified the γ2a CH domain sequence from cDNA generated from the hybridomas producing the K28/43 IgG2a mAb and then replaced the γ1 CH domain present in the K28/43R plasmid with this γ2a CH domain using standard cloning.
evidence: This is a description of the methodology used.

claim: The authors have successfully cloned and validated as functional R-mAbs a total of 178 mAbs.
source: Toward this end, we have successfully cloned and validated as functional R-mAbs a total of 178 mAbs (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a summary statistic from the authors' data referenced in Supplementary file 2.

claim: The 178 successfully cloned R-mAbs include 148 mAbs of distinct subclasses converted to IgG2a R-mAbs (125 IgG1, 21 IgG2b, and 3 IgG3), and 29 IgG2a mAbs that were retained in their native IgG subclass.
source: This includes 148 mAbs of distinct subclasses converted to IgG2a R-mAbs (125 IgG1, 21 IgG2b, and 3 IgG3), and 29 IgG2a mAbs that were retained in their native IgG subclass (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a summary statistic from the authors' data referenced in Supplementary file 2.

claim: Each of the 178 R-mAbs have been assigned unique RRID numbers in the Antibody Registry.
source: Each of these R-mAbs have been assigned unique RRID numbers in the Antibody Registry (Supplementary file 2) and all will be deposited in plasmid form at Addgene, a subset of which are already available (https://www.addgene.org/James_Trimmer/).
evidence: This is stated in the text and referenced in Supplementary file 2.

claim: Subclass switching allowed Nav channel labeling at nodes to be verified by co-labeling with K65/35 an IgG1 subclass antibody directed against CASPR.
source: Importantly, subclass switching allowed Nav channel labeling at nodes to be verified by co-labeling with K65/35 an IgG1 subclass antibody directed against CASPR, a protein concentrated at paranodes (Menegoz et al., 1997; Peles et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A and citations to Menegoz et al., 1997 and Peles et al., 1997.

claim: Simultaneous labeling for the highly-related GABA-A receptor β1 and β3 subunits could not be performed with their respective mAbs N96/55 and N87/25 as both are IgG1 subclass.
source: Similarly, simultaneous labeling for the highly-related GABA-A receptor β1 and β3 subunits (Zhang et al., 1991) with their widely used respective mAbs N96/55 and N87/25 could not be performed as both are IgG1 subclass.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the IgG subclass of the mAbs and citation to Zhang et al., 1991.

claim: Switching the N96/55 mAb to the IgG2a N96/55R R-mAb allowed simultaneous detection of GABA-A receptor β1 and β3 subunits.
source: Switching the N96/55 mAb to the IgG2a N96/55R R-mAb allowed simultaneous detection of these two highly-related but distinct GABA-A receptor subunits.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In Figure 4B localization of GABA-A receptor β1 and β3 subunits appeared completely non-overlapping in separate layers of cerebellum.
source: In Figure 4B localization of GABA-A receptor β1 and β3 subunits appeared completely non-overlapping in separate layers of cerebellum.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The D3/71 mAb has particular value in binding at a site distinct from other anti-Kv2.1 mAbs, which remains intact in truncated isoforms of Kv2.1 found in patients with severe neurodevelopmental disorders linked to de novo frameshift or nonsense mutations in the KCNB1 gene.
source: The D3/71 mAb has particular value in binding at a site distinct from other anti-Kv2.1 mAbs, which unlike most other available anti-Kv2.1 mAbs (and pAbs), remains intact in truncated isoforms of Kv2.1 found in patients with severe neurodevelopmental disorders linked to de novo frameshift or nonsense mutations in the KCNB1 gene (de Kovel et al., 2016; Marini et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to de Kovel et al., 2016 and Marini et al., 2017.

claim: When the authors attempted to resuscitate the cryopreserved D3/71 hybridoma cell line over 20 years after it was cryopreserved, the cells were no longer viable.
source: Unlike our experience with other cryopreserved hybridomas in our collection, when we attempted to resuscitate this cryopreserved hybridoma cell line over 20 years after it was cryopreserved, the D3/71 hybridoma cells were no longer viable.
evidence: This is a description of the authors' observation.

claim: The authors extracted RNA from a cryopreserved vial of D3/71 hybridoma cells in an attempt to generate a functional D3/71R R-mAb.
source: We extracted RNA from a cryopreserved vial of D3/71 hybridoma cells in an attempt to generate a functional D3/71R R-mAb.
evidence: This is a description of the methodology used.

claim: Most of the bacterial colonies tested (20/24) were positive for the insert by PCR.
source: Most of the bacterial colonies tested (20/24) were positive for the insert by PCR (Figure 5C), and subsequent restriction analysis of 12 of these positive clones confirmed that they each contained the full-length VL-joining fragment-VH cassette (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: A subset of the recovered and subclass-switched D3/71R R-mAbs were positive in the COS-1-ICC assay.
source: A subset of the recovered and subclass-switched D3/71R R-mAbs were positive in this assay (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The D3/71R R-mAb exhibits immunolabeling of endogenous Kv2.1 in neurons in mouse neocortex that recapitulates the previously established pattern of Kv2.1 immunolabeling in these neurons.
source: Moreover, the D3/71R R-mAb exhibits immunolabeling of endogenous Kv2.1 in neurons in mouse neocortex that recapitulates the previously established pattern of Kv2.1 immunolabeling in these neurons (e.g., Bishop et al., 2015; Trimmer, 1991; Rhodes et al., 1995) and that overlaps precisely with simultaneous immunolabeling obtained with the native K89/34 mAb (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C and citations to Bishop et al., 2015; Trimmer, 1991; Rhodes et al., 1995.

claim: The D3/71R R-mAb yields an immunoreactive band on immunoblots similar to that obtained with K89/34 and K89/34R.
source: The D3/71R R-mAb also yields an immunoreactive band on immunoblots similar to that obtained with K89/34 and K89/34R (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The mAb cloning approach described can be used to effectively recover functional R-mAbs from non-viable hybridomas.
source: These results suggest that the mAb cloning approach described here can be used to effectively recover functional R-mAbs from non-viable hybridomas and could be applied by researchers that have such hybridomas in their collections.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the D3/71R data.

claim: Varying degrees of allelic exclusion in the hybridomas could contribute to the variable efficiency of whether colony PCR and restriction enzyme assay-positive clones would produce an R-mAb that recapitulated immunolabeling obtained with the native mAb.
source: Varying degrees of allelic exclusion in the hybridomas that served as the source of our R-mAbs could also contribute to the variable efficiency of whether colony PCR and restriction enzyme assay-positive clones would produce an R-mAb that recapitulated immunolabeling obtained with the native mAb.
evidence: This is a speculation based on prior literature about allelic exclusion in hybridomas.

claim: A lack of allelic exclusion at heavy and light chain IgG loci has been documented in hybridomas, resulting in expression of multiple IgG heavy and/or light chains at the mRNA and protein levels.
source: Moreover, a lack of allelic exclusion at heavy and light chain IgG loci has been documented in hybridomas, resulting in expression of multiple IgG heavy and/or light chains at the mRNA and protein levels (Zack et al., 1995; Blatt et al., 1998; Bradbury et al., 2018; Ruberti et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Zack et al., 1995; Blatt et al., 1998; Bradbury et al., 2018; Ruberti et al., 1994.

claim: In previous studies, while multiple combinations of heavy and light IgG chains were produced by monoclonal hybridoma cells, only one combination produced an R-mAb capable of recognizing the target antigen.
source: In these previous studies, while multiple combinations of heavy and light IgG chains were produced by monoclonal hybridoma cells, only one combination of heavy and light IgG chains present in the hybridoma produced an R-mAb capable of recognizing the target antigen.
evidence: This claim is based on prior literature about hybridoma antibody production.

claim: The vast majority (84%) of the 114 projects for which ≥ 4 clones were evaluated yielded at least one positive R-mAb.
source: That the vast majority (84%) of the 114 projects for which ≥ 4 clones were evaluated yielded at least one positive R-mAb suggests that the presence of a small and variable number of negative clones does not impact the overall success of the approach described here, given the simple but effective nature of microplate screening assays, such as the ICC assay employed here, to rapidly and easily screen candidate R-mAbs.
evidence: This is a summary statistic and inference from the authors' data.

claim: There is a growing impetus to enhance research reproducibility by both improving the quality of Abs used in basic research and in diagnostics, and the transparency of their reporting.
source: There is a growing impetus to enhance research reproducibility by both improving the quality of Abs used in basic research and in diagnostics, and the transparency of their reporting as related to the exact molecularly-defined Ab that was used (Taussig et al., 2018; Bradbury and Plückthun, 2015; Uhlen et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Taussig et al., 2018; Bradbury and Plückthun, 2015; Uhlen et al., 2016.

claim: Using mAbs in their recombinant form and defining them unambiguously at the molecular level by publishing their VL and VH domain sequences is a step towards achieving enhanced reproducibility.
source: Using mAbs in their recombinant form and defining them unambiguously at the molecular level by publishing their VL and VH domain sequences is a step towards achieving this goal and elevate reproducibility world-wide.
evidence: This is an inference based on the advantages of molecular definition.

claim: Polyclonal Ab preparations have unique benefits due to the presence of Abs recognizing distinct epitopes on the target protein.
source: Among the different forms of research and diagnostic Abs, polyclonal Ab preparations have unique benefits (Ascoli and Aggeler, 2018), due to the presence of Abs recognizing distinct epitopes on the target protein.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ascoli and Aggeler, 2018.

claim: Polyclonal Abs are inherently limited by their intrinsic lack of precise molecular definition.
source: However, in any of the diverse forms in which they are available (antiserum, IgG fractions, affinity-purified) polyclonal Abs are inherently limited by their intrinsic lack of precise molecular definition.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the nature of polyclonal antibodies.

claim: The inability to rigorously define the clonal composition of specific preparations can contribute to batch-to-batch variation in the efficacy and specificity of the polyclonal collection for any specific application.
source: The inability to rigorously define the clonal composition of specific preparations can contribute to batch-to-batch variation in the efficacy and specificity of the polyclonal collection for any specific application, negatively impacting the reproducibility of research performed with such Abs.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the heterogeneity of polyclonal antibodies.

claim: Unlike mAbs, polyclonal Abs are a finite resource whose depletion can lead to batch-to-batch variability or complete lack of availability.
source: Moreover, unlike mAbs, polyclonal Abs are a finite resource whose depletion can lead to batch-to-batch variability or complete lack of availability, stymieing independent reproduction of research using the same reagent.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the nature of polyclonal antibody production.

claim: Conventional mAbs are advantageous in lacking the molecular complexity of polyclonal preparations, and in being renewable reagents.
source: Conventional mAbs are advantageous in lacking the molecular complexity of polyclonal preparations, and in being renewable reagents.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the nature of monoclonal antibodies.

claim: The conversion of conventional hybridoma-generated mAbs into R-mAbs offers numerous additional advantages including ensuring their broad availability by generating a publicly accessible DNA sequence archive.
source: However, the conversion of conventional hybridoma-generated mAbs into R-mAbs offers numerous additional advantages. This includes ensuring their broad availability by generating a publicly accessible DNA sequence archive that can be used to synthesize the functional VL and VH domain sequences.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the properties of DNA sequences.

claim: R-mAbs are more easily distributed as plasmids or DNA sequence, a feature that should enhance dissemination of this resource, relative to the more labile cryopreserved and/or living hybridomas.
source: R-mAbs are also more easily distributed as plasmids or DNA sequence, a feature that should enhance dissemination of this resource, relative to the more labile cryopreserved and/or living hybridomas that are less amenable to long-distance transport.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the stability of DNA versus living cells.

claim: Cloning enhances research reproducibility by the unambiguous definition of mAbs at the level of their cDNA sequence.
source: Cloning also enhances research reproducibility by the unambiguous definition of mAbs at the level of their cDNA sequence, as well as the enhanced control of molecular composition afforded by expressing a single light and heavy chain combination from transfected cells and their high-level animal-free production in cell culture.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the molecular definition provided by cloning.

claim: Cloning of mAbs allows for increased utility as offered by their subsequent engineering into alternate forms, such as the subclass-switched R-mAbs generated here.
source: Cloning of mAbs also allows for increased utility as offered by their subsequent engineering into alternate forms, such as the subclass-switched R-mAbs generated here.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in the manuscript showing subclass-switched R-mAbs.

claim: The method described represents a straightforward approach to producing functional R-mAbs from existing murine hybridomas that could be applied to other valuable mAb collections.
source: The method described here represents a straightforward approach to producing functional R-mAbs from existing murine hybridomas that could be applied to other valuable mAb collections to ensure their permanent archiving, which cannot be assured when they exist solely in the form of hybridomas cryopreserved in liquid nitrogen.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the successful application of the method.

claim: There are many cases of important hybridomas, including entire collections, that have been discarded upon the closure of the laboratory that formerly housed and financially supported the maintenance of the cryopreserved collection.
source: In particular, there are many cases of important hybridomas, including entire collections, that have been discarded upon the closure of the laboratory that formerly housed and financially supported the maintenance of the cryopreserved collection.
evidence: This is a general observation about the field.

claim: Simple conversion of mAbs to R-mAbs paves the way for higher throughput approaches, for example those employing high throughput 'next generation' sequencing to simultaneously obtain light and heavy chain sequences from large pools of hybridomas.
source: Simple conversion of mAbs to R-mAbs, as described here, also paves the way for higher throughput approaches, for example those employing high throughput 'next generation' sequencing to simultaneously obtain light and heavy chain sequences from large pools of hybridomas (Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculation about future applications supported by citation to Chen et al., 2018.

claim: Next generation sequencing should allow for larger scale 'en masse' conversion efforts more suitable to large hybridoma collections.
source: In theory this should allow for larger scale 'en masse' (as opposed to the mAb-by-mAb approach used here) conversion efforts more suitable to large hybridoma collections.
evidence: This is a speculation about future applications.

claim: The authors' larger collection comprises ≈40,000 target-specific mAbs archived in their cryopreserved hybridoma collection.
source: For example, our larger collection of ≈40,000 target-specific mAbs archived in our cryopreserved hybridoma collection, and other widely used collections, such as that housed at the Developmental Studies Hybridoma Bank (http://dshb.biology.uiowa.edu/; comprising 3,672 mAbs as of 9/9/18) might represent appropriate targets for such next generation sequencing approaches.
evidence: This is a statement about the authors' collection.

claim: The Developmental Studies Hybridoma Bank comprises 3,672 mAbs as of 9/9/18.
source: For example, our larger collection of ≈40,000 target-specific mAbs archived in our cryopreserved hybridoma collection, and other widely used collections, such as that housed at the Developmental Studies Hybridoma Bank (http://dshb.biology.uiowa.edu/; comprising 3,672 mAbs as of 9/9/18) might represent appropriate targets for such next generation sequencing approaches.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the DSHB collection.

claim: Future efforts to generate R-mAbs from cryopreserved hybridoma collections will further enhance the rigor, reproducibility and overall effectiveness of Ab-based research.
source: Future efforts to generate R-mAbs from cryopreserved hybridoma collections will further enhance the rigor, reproducibility and overall effectiveness of Ab-based research.
evidence: This is a conclusion and speculation about future impact.

source: Frozen vials containing 0.5–1 × 107 hybridoma cells per vial were thawed in a 37°C water bath for 5 min, in batches of 20 vials for high through-put purposes.
evidence: This is a description of the methodology used.

claim: The authors used 1–3 × 106 cells for RNA extraction.
source: A 250 µL aliquot of this cell suspension, representing 1–3 × 106 cells, was used for RNA extraction according to the manufacturer's instructions.
evidence: This is a description of the methodology used.

source: As such, the templates for the VH and VL domain PCR amplification represented the cDNA yield from ≈3,000–7,500 hybridoma cells.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the methodology described.

source: Briefly, degenerate primer sets were used to amplify mouse Ig kappa VL and VH sequences using PFU Ultra II Fusion HS DNA polymerase (Agilent Technologies Cat# 600670) and Advantage 2 Polymerase Mix (ClonTech Cat# 639201) for VL and VH amplification, respectively.
evidence: This is a description of the methodology used.

evidence: This is a description of cell line authentication.

evidence: This is a description of quality control testing.

claim: The ThermoFisher Scientific mouse mAb catalog comprises 69% IgG1, 18% IgG2a and 12% IgG2b as of 6/28/18.
source: As a prominent example, the large mouse mAb catalog of ThermoFisher Scientific (10,992 independent IgG mouse mAbs as of 6/28/18) follows this remarkably closely, comprising 69% IgG1, 18% IgG2a and 12% IgG2b (Matt Baker, ThermoFisher Scientific, personal communication).

source: In general, mouse mAb collections reflect the representation of these subclasses in the circulating serum IgGs in immunized BALB/c mice, which is ≈70% IgG1, ≈20% IgG2a and ≈10% IgG2b (Natsuume-Sakai et al., 1977).

source: As one example, interrogating the Abs registered with the Antibody Registry (2,381,068 as of 9/9/18) shows a preponderance (84% in total) of Abs raised in only three species: rabbits (44.6%), mice (31.2%) and goats (8.2%), with all other species together accounting for the remaining 16%.

claim: Among the predominant species, goat Abs are exclusively polyclonal and as such cannot be used with one another in simultaneous multiplex labeling.
source: Among the predominant species, goat Abs are exclusively polyclonal and as such cannot be used with one another in simultaneous multiplex labeling.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the nature of polyclonal antibodies.

claim: The bulk of secondary Abs are raised in goats, constraining facile detection of primary Abs in multiplex labeling experiments employing goat primary Abs.
source: Moreover, the bulk of secondary Abs are raised in goats, constraining facile detection of primary Abs in multiplex labeling experiments employing goat primary Abs.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the common use of goat secondary antibodies.

claim: Employing multiple goat or rabbit primary Abs for multiplex immunolabeling involves costly and time-consuming procedures such as direct labeling with different fluorophores or sequential multiplexing technologies such as Opal.
source: As such employing multiple goat or rabbit primary Abs for multiplex immunolabeling involves costly and time-consuming procedures such as direct labeling with different fluorophores or sequential multiplexing technologies such as Opal (Stack et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Stack et al., 2014.

claim: Multiplex labeling using the classical approach of employing primary Abs raised in different species and their subsequent detection with species-specific secondary Abs is highly limited by the lack of available Abs from numerous species.

claim: Simultaneous multiplex labeling of multiple targets within a single sample allows for better comparison of their relative levels, co-localization, and overall tissue architecture.

evidence: This is a logical inference based on the advantages of multiplex labeling.

claim: Multiplex labeling conserves valuable samples, as multiple targets can be interrogated in the same sample instead of across multiple samples.
source: Multiplex labeling also conserves valuable samples, as multiple targets can be interrogated in the same sample instead of across multiple samples, which can be a particular concern in studies using human tissue samples that may be available in limited quantity.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the advantages of multiplex labeling.

claim: The authors previously undertook a systematic analysis of anti-mouse IgG subclass-specific secondary antibodies and demonstrated their use for simultaneous multiplex immunolabeling.
source: We previously undertook a systematic analysis of anti-mouse IgG subclass-specific secondary antibodies and demonstrated that the use of mouse mAbs of different IgG subclasses in combination with anti-mouse IgG subclass-specific secondary antibodies for simultaneous multiplex immunolabeling allows for robust and specific labeling in several immunolabeling applications, and also provides enhanced signal-to-noise (background) in immunolabeling of brain samples when compared to generic anti-mouse IgG (H + L) secondary Abs (Bekele-Arcuri et al., 1996; Rhodes et al., 1997; Lim et al., 2000; Rasband et al., 2001; Manning et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple prior publications from the authors' group.
